newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Rhone-Poulenc studies buyout of Rorer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rhone-Poulenc studies buyout of Rorer.

text.p: French drugs and chemicals group Rhone-Poulenc said on Thursday it was considering launching a 25 billion franc ($4.3 billion) bid to buy the outstanding shares of Rhone-Poulenc Rorer, in which it currently holds a 68.3 percent stake.

It said it also wanted to regroup its chemical and fibre operations into a single new unit, which would then be spun off and taken public in 1998. The move would be aimed at exploiting the units' technological, industrial and commercial synergies, the company said.

Analysts said the moves made strategic sense and were in line with Rhone's ambitions to concentrate on its lucrative pharmaceuticals business. They said the takeover would be slightly dilutive to earnings.
Rhone said it would pay Rhone Poulenc Rorer's (RPR) minority shareholders $92 per share in the deal. RPR stock closed just over $79 per share on the New York Stock Exchange on Wednesday.
A company official said Rhone Poulenc stopped short of an outright offer today because under a 1990 standstill agreement, Rhone Poulenc cannot increase its holding in RPR until after July 31, 1997.

"We are announcing this now because we have carried out enough studies to be able to announce our intention to the markets with a concern for transparency...but we cannot advance a final decision because of the standstill agreement and because we have not completely finished our studies," Rhone Poulenc Managing Director Igor Landau told Reuters in an interview on Thursday after the announcement.

Rhone Poulenc shareholders reacted well to the news, bidding the stock up so sharply that it was suspended limit up at the opening of the Paris bourse. The share closed at 211.9 francs on Wednesday and was trading at 241.2, up 13.83 percent by 0856 GMT on Thursday.
In a statement, the firm estimated the cost of the transaction at 25 billion francs.

Landau said the company would finance the the buyout with a seven billion franc capital increase, asset sales, income from the market flotation of the new chemicals and fibre unit and from improved annual cash flow after the deal.

"For the 25 billion (that the deal should cost) there will be a capital increase of seven billion francs and the income from our strategic sales as well as the income from the sale on the market of part of the new chemicals company," Landau said.
"These represent about 13 billion francs so on the 25 billion we would have 20 billion and the rest would come from improved annual cash flow."
Landau conceded that the takeover "is a little dilutive the first year, a little less the second and not at all, on the contrary, from year three."
"The dilution is slight enough so that we were able to confirm excepting exceptional elements, the 20 percent growth of our profits in 1997 and 1998," he added.
In the statement released by the company, chairman Jean-Renne Fourtou said the deal would help the company and its shareholders.
"These measures would make up a new and important step in the transformation of Rhone-Poulenc into one of the world's leaders in life sciences," he said.
Rhone-Poulenc said its debt to shareholders' equity ratio would be reduced to 60 percent at the end of 1998 and 50 percent at the end of 1999.
It said the net debt linked to the rise of its stake in Rhone-Poulenc Rorer would be quickly reduced through such measures as improved operating cash flow and an increase in shareholders' equity.
Rhone-Poulenc reaffirmed an earlier estimate that its net profit per share would increase by 20 percent for 1997 and 1998, despite a weak dilution and excluding exceptional items.
In 1996, Rhone Poulenc earned 2.74 billion francs in 1996 or 8.44 francs per share compared to 6.71 francs in 1995.
It said it expected to maintain in 1997 the dividend it paid in 1996. In 1996 it paid 5.25 francs per share gross dividend.
